## Why This Matters

An MLP sees an image the way you would see a shuffled bag of its pixels: it **flattens** the 28x28
grid into 784 numbers and forgets which pixel sat next to which. Yet everything that makes a shoe a
shoe is *spatial* -- edges, curves, the relationship between neighboring pixels. The analogy: reading
a page by being handed its letters in a random pile versus reading them in place.

A **convolution** reads the image *in place*. It slides a small **filter** -- a magnifying glass
tuned to one pattern, like a vertical edge -- across the picture, and at every location reports how
strongly that pattern is present. Because the same magnifying glass is reused everywhere, a CNN
learns a pattern **once** and can spot it **anywhere**, using a handful of weights instead of one per
pixel. That single idea, inspired by the visual cortex (Hubel & Wiesel) and proven by LeCun's LeNet-5
on handwritten digits, is what makes deep learning work on images.

## The Problem with Flattening

The L15 MLP flattens an image to a vector and wires every pixel to every hidden unit. Two costs
follow. First, **parameters explode**: a dense layer from 784 pixels to 784 units already has over
600,000 weights, and real images are far larger. Second, there is **no translation invariance**: a
weight that learned "edge here, top-left" knows nothing about the same edge bottom-right -- the MLP
must relearn every pattern at every position. Convolution removes both costs at once.

## The Convolutional Layer

A neuron in a convolutional layer is **not** connected to every pixel -- only to a small **local
receptive field**, a patch of the input. Its weights form a **filter** (or **kernel**), a small
matrix that is **slid across the whole image**. At each position you multiply the filter by the patch
it covers and sum -- that is the **convolution operation** -- producing one number. Sweep the filter
over every position and the numbers form a **feature map**: a picture of *where in the image that
filter's pattern fires*.

Two knobs set the output size: the **stride** (how far the filter steps each move) and **zero-padding**
(adding a border of zeros so the output can keep the input's height and width). The decisive property
is **parameter sharing**: the *same* filter weights are used at every position. So a 3x3 filter is
just nine weights (plus a bias), no matter how large the image -- and whatever pattern it learns is
detected **anywhere** it appears. That is **translation invariance**, and it is exactly what an MLP
lacks.

## Channels and Stacking

Images have **channels** -- depth: 1 for grayscale, 3 for RGB. A filter always spans *all* input
channels (a 3x3 filter on an RGB image is really 3x3x3 weights). A single filter detects a single
pattern, so a convolutional layer holds **many** filters, each producing its own feature map. The
layer's output is therefore a stack of feature maps -- its own depth, fed as the channels of the next
layer. Early layers learn low-level patterns (edges, blobs); later layers combine them into a
**feature hierarchy** -- parts, then whole objects.

## Pooling

A **pooling layer** subsamples each feature map over small windows -- typically taking the **max** in
each 2x2 window (**max pooling**; **average pooling** takes the mean). Pooling has **no weights**; it
just shrinks the height and width (**subsampling**), which cuts compute and memory and adds a little
more translation invariance (the exact position of a feature matters less). A common block is
therefore `Conv -> ReLU -> Pool`, repeated to build depth while shrinking the spatial size.

## A CNN, End to End

Stack a couple of `Conv -> ReLU -> Pool` blocks to extract a feature hierarchy, then `Flatten` the
final feature maps and finish with one or two **dense** layers ending in **logits** -- the exact same
output as L15, paired with `CrossEntropyLoss`. The filters are not designed by hand; they are
**learned by backprop** (L16), and the whole net trains with the same loop (L15) and tricks (L17).
The only new bookkeeping is the **spatial trace** -- watch the size shrink so you know the flattened
dimension:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  inp["input<br/>1 x 28 x 28"] --> c1["Conv 3x3 x32<br/>+ ReLU"]
  c1 --> p1["MaxPool 2<br/>32 x 14 x 14"]
  p1 --> c2["Conv 3x3 x64<br/>+ ReLU"]
  c2 --> p2["MaxPool 2<br/>64 x 7 x 7"]
  p2 --> fl["Flatten<br/>3136"]
  fl --> d1["Dense 128<br/>+ ReLU"]
  d1 --> out["Dense 10<br/>logits"]
```

The lab builds exactly this network. Its two convolutional layers hold only **320** and **18,496**
weights -- a few hundred to a few thousand, because the filters are shared -- while the dense head
holds most of the rest. Trained on Fashion-MNIST it reaches **0.889** test accuracy, beating the
L15-style MLP's **0.860** on the same images: the CNN wins because convolution and pooling exploit the
2-D structure and translation invariance an MLP throws away.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Flattening too early.** Flatten only *after* the convolutional layers have extracted spatial
  features; flatten the raw image and you are back to an MLP.
- **Forgetting the tensor layout.** PyTorch images are **NCHW** (batch, channels, height, width); a
  `Conv2d` expects a 4-D tensor, not a flat vector.
- **The wrong flattened dimension.** The first dense layer's input size must match the flattened
  feature maps (here 64 x 7 x 7 = 3136). Trace the spatial size, or let `nn.LazyLinear` infer it.
- **Thinking pooling "learns."** Pooling has **no weights** -- it only subsamples. All the learning is
  in the convolutional and dense layers.
- **Expecting a CNN to need *more* data than an MLP.** Parameter sharing means it needs *less* per
  pattern -- it sees the same pattern everywhere with one filter.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why does a CNN beat an MLP on images?"** -- Two reasons: it keeps the 2-D structure (neighboring
pixels stay neighbors), and parameter sharing lets one filter detect a pattern anywhere, so it
generalizes from far less data than a dense net that must relearn every position.

**"How big should a filter be?"** -- Small (3x3 is the modern default); stacking several small filters
sees a large region while using fewer weights than one big filter. The lab uses 3x3.

**"Conv or pooling for downsampling?"** -- Pooling is the classic way (cheap, no parameters); many
modern nets instead use a strided convolution. Either shrinks the spatial size; the lab uses max
pooling for clarity.

**"Where do real architectures go from here?"** -- Deeper stacks with clever wiring -- residual
connections (ResNet), inception blocks -- and **transfer learning** from models pretrained on millions
of images. That is L19. Training those at scale (GPU, augmentation) is the CDAT 4013 lab's territory.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Convolutional layer | slide a small filter over local receptive fields; weights shared across positions |
| Filter / kernel | the small learnable weight matrix; one filter = one pattern detector |
| Feature map | a filter's output: where in the image that pattern fires |
| Stride / padding | step size of the filter / zero-border to control output size |
| Parameter sharing | one filter reused everywhere -> few weights + translation invariance |
| Channels / stacking | input depth (1 gray, 3 RGB); many filters -> many feature maps |
| Pooling | subsample each feature map (max common); no weights; shrinks H and W |
| Feature hierarchy | stacked conv layers: edges -> parts -> objects |
| The recipe | `Conv -> ReLU -> Pool` blocks, then `Flatten -> Dense -> logits` |
